overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Heidegger's turn from consciousness to the question of being. You'll be asked about the ontological difference, Dasein, facticity, Heidegger's definition of phenomenology, and his objection to Husserl's transcendental subject.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A physicist measures the mass of an electron. A philosopher asks what it is for something to be a physical thing at all. How does Heidegger classify the two inquiries?

options.html: Both are ontological, since both concern what exists
options.text: Both are ontological, since both concern what exists
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Measuring an electron's mass concerns a particular being and its properties, which makes it ontic. Only the philosopher's question is about being.

options.html: The first is ontic, and the second is ontological
options.text: The first is ontic, and the second is ontological
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The physicist studies a being and its properties. The philosopher asks about the being of beings, which is the ontological question.

options.html: The first is ontological, and the second is ontic
options.text: The first is ontological, and the second is ontic
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. It's the reverse. Questions about a particular being's properties are ontic. Questions about the being of beings are ontological.

options.html: Both are ontic, since both concern particular beings
options.text: Both are ontic, since both concern particular beings
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The philosopher's question isn't about a particular being. It asks what it is to be a physical thing, which is ontological.

forms.stemHtml: How does Heidegger define phenomenology in Being and Time §7?

options.html: As the science of the mental images that represent outer things
options.text: As the science of the mental images that represent outer things
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. For Heidegger, phenomenology lets what shows itself be seen from itself. It isn't a science of mental images.

options.html: As the study of appearances that point to hidden things in themselves
options.text: As the study of appearances that point to hidden things in themselves
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger defines phenomenology as letting what shows itself be seen from itself. He distinguishes phenomena from appearances that point beyond themselves.

options.html: As letting what shows itself be seen from itself, as it shows itself
options.text: As letting what shows itself be seen from itself, as it shows itself
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Phenomenology names a method, not a subject matter. What it most needs to bring into view is the being of beings, which is usually hidden.

options.html: As the explanation of experiences by their causes in the brain
options.text: As the explanation of experiences by their causes in the brain
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger defines phenomenology as a method of letting what shows itself be seen from itself, not as causal explanation.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following describe Dasein's facticity? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Finding yourself already speaking a particular language
options.text: Finding yourself already speaking a particular language
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Facticity is finding yourself already in a world and situation you didn't choose.

options.html: Being born into a family and a history you didn't choose
options.text: Being born into a family and a history you didn't choose
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Facticity includes the situation you always already find yourself in.

options.html: Being contained in a room the way water is in a glass
options.text: Being contained in a room the way water is in a glass
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's spatial inclusion, which Heidegger contrasts with Dasein's being-in-the-world.

options.html: Being bound up with the beings you meet in your world
options.text: Being bound up with the beings you meet in your world
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Heidegger describes facticity as Dasein's being bound up with the beings it meets in its world.

options.html: Having a measurable height and weight, like a stone
options.text: Having a measurable height and weight, like a stone
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A stone's being-there is a mere fact. Dasein's facticity is lived: finding itself already in a world.

forms.stemHtml: What is Heidegger's term for the kind of being we ourselves are: the being whose own being is an issue for it? Enter one word.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Heidegger chose "Dasein" to avoid the ontology built into terms such as "subject" and "consciousness."
Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger avoids "subject" because it treats the self as a thing with properties. His term is "Dasein."

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger's term for the being whose own being is an issue for it is "Dasein."

forms.stemHtml: What is Heidegger's main objection to starting phenomenology from Husserl's transcendental subject?

options.html: It relies on scientific data that phenomenology should avoid
options.text: It relies on scientific data that phenomenology should avoid
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger's objection is that intentionality presupposes being-in-the-world, so the transcendental subject is an abstraction.

options.html: It denies that experience is directed at objects at all
options.text: It denies that experience is directed at objects at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl's subject is defined by intentionality. Heidegger's objection is that intentionality presupposes being-in-the-world.

options.html: It treats the world as a construct of language alone
options.text: It treats the world as a construct of language alone
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger's objection is that intentionality presupposes being-in-the-world, so the transcendental subject abstracts from it.

options.html: It abstracts from our prior involvement in a world
options.text: It abstracts from our prior involvement in a world
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On Heidegger's view, intentionality presupposes being-in-the-world, and the transcendental subject is an abstraction from it.

title: The Question of Being
